An interactive exhibit

Violence, Gender and Control

How enslavers used violence shaped by gender in the American South before the Civil War.

Research question

How did enslavers use physical and sexual violence to establish and maintain gender-based power and control over enslaved men and women in the American South before the Civil War?

Thesis

Enslavers in the American South before the Civil War did not use one kind of violence on one kind of body. They matched physical and sexual violence to gender, because gender influenced what they could take from each body: labour, children, or both. Enslaved people's resistance shows that this control was never complete.

Content note This site discusses physical and sexual violence under slavery. It shows historical paintings, sculpture, a photograph and a document from the period, none of them graphic. You can move through it at your own pace and leave any room at any time.

Efrain Obazee
SOCSCI 1SS3 Engaging Literature, McMaster University
Dr. J. Gouweloos. Course theme: critical studies of crime and criminalization.

The puzzle

One violence, or two?

Most accounts of slavery describe violence against enslaved people as one shared experience. My puzzle is why enslavers' violence took different forms for men and women, and what that difference reveals about how enslavers held power.

Five rooms

Choose a room

Enter the rooms in any order. Each room presents claims from the literature, then my analysis. The conclusion opens after you have visited all five.

0 of 5 rooms visited

Room 1 of 5

Forced reproduction

Open each card to read what the source shows.

  • According to Djelid (2024), enslavers forced enslaved men and women to reproduce.

  • Djelid (2024) writes that enslavers used "a spectrum of violence as a tool of coercion" (Djelid, 2024, p. 21).

  • As Djelid (2024) shows, enslavers selected people for desired traits and exploited their children.

  • Djelid (2024) also notes that some enslaved men were hired out or kept as "stock men" (Djelid, 2024, p. ___).

My analysis

Djelid's evidence shows that sexual violence under slavery did not target women alone. Enslavers treated reproduction as a business decision and used violence to force it on men and women. Fausto-Sterling (2000/2018) explains Foucault's idea of bio-power, where those in power manage bodies and control births across a population. Forced reproduction was bio-power carried out with a whip.

Room 2 of 5

Mothers

Open each card to read what the source shows.

  • According to West and Shearer (2018), slaveholders exploited enslaved mothers as both workers and reproducers.

  • West and Shearer (2018) explain that law made the child of an enslaved woman enslaved.

  • West and Shearer (2018) note that some pregnancies resulted from sexual assault.

  • West and Shearer (2018) also show that motherhood was a source of pride and shared, communal care.

  • In the words of West and Shearer (2018), "motherhood could be a double-edged sword for women in bondage" (West & Shearer, 2018, p. 1008).

My analysis

West and Shearer show that enslavers expected women to work and bear children at the same time. Fausto-Sterling's table of dualisms helps explain how enslavers justified this. The table pairs master with slave, male with female, and production with reproduction (Fausto-Sterling, 2000/2018, p. 137). Enslaved women were placed on the lower side of every pair, so enslavers claimed both their labour and their bodies. Motherhood gave enslaved women pride and connection, but it was also the reason enslavers valued them.

Room 3 of 5

Men

Open each card to read what the source shows.

  • According to Doddington (2018), enslaved men "crafted a masculine identity through work" (Doddington, 2018, p. 288).

  • Doddington (2018) shows that expectations of enslaved men changed as they aged.

  • Doddington (2018) also finds that community support was not always offered.

  • According to Djelid (2024), enslavers also controlled men's sexual and reproductive lives.

My analysis

Doddington shows that enslaved men built identities through work even while enslavers controlled their lives. Djelid shows that this control reached into men's sexual and reproductive lives. Together, these sources show that slavery did not erase masculinity. Enslavers shaped and limited it, and it shifted as men aged. Fausto-Sterling (2000/2018) argues that labelling someone a man or a woman is a social decision. Under slavery, enslavers made many of those decisions for the people they owned.

Room 4 of 5

Resistance

Open each card to read what the source shows.

  • According to Shearer (2025), enslaved women turned everyday objects into weapons against overseers.

  • Shearer (2025) finds that their violence sometimes went beyond self-defense into retribution.

  • Shearer (2025) states that "Black female-perpetrated violence was not solely defensive" (Shearer, 2025, p. 264).

  • Shearer (2025) draws on judicial records, fugitive narratives and testimony of the formerly enslaved.

My analysis

Shearer's research challenges the idea that enslaved women were only victims of violence. They used everyday objects as weapons, and some struck back for past abuse. This breaks the dualism of the active master and the passive slave. This supports the last part of my thesis. Enslavers used violence to control enslaved people, but that control was never complete.

Room 5 of 5

Law and crime

Open each card to read what the source shows.

  • According to West and Shearer (2018), law made the child of an enslaved woman enslaved, which gave enslavers a financial reason to control reproduction.

  • Shearer (2025) shows that enslaved women's violent resistance appears in judicial records.

  • According to Fausto-Sterling (2000/2018, p. 136), Foucault gave "discipline" a double meaning, both control or punishment and an academic body of knowledge.

My analysis

This room connects my research to crime and criminalization. Slavery used discipline in both of Foucault's senses (Fausto-Sterling, 2000/2018). The law turned enslaved women's children into property (West & Shearer, 2018). The everyday violence enslavers used was part of how the system ran. When enslaved women used violence, it appeared in judicial records (Shearer, 2025). This difference shows how law decided whose violence counted as a problem.

Conclusion

What the difference reveals

Enslavers in the American South before the Civil War did not use one kind of violence on one kind of body. They matched physical and sexual violence to gender, because gender influenced what they could take from each body: labour, children, or both. Enslaved people's resistance shows that this control was never complete.

Fausto-Sterling argues that "ideas of both race and gender emerge from wider-lying assumptions" about the body (2000/2018, p. 136). Slavery shows how violent those assumptions could become. The resistance of enslaved people shows the limits of that power.
